chapters.1: John the Baptist prepares the way in the wilderness, and Jesus is baptized by him and then tested by Satan for forty days. Jesus calls his first disciples (Simon, Andrew, James, and John) by the Sea of Galilee, teaches with striking authority in the Capernaum synagogue, and casts out an unclean spirit there. He goes on to heal Simon's mother-in-law, many other sick and demon-possessed people, and a leper, and his fame spreads quickly through the region.
chapters.2: Jesus forgives and heals a paralyzed man lowered through a roof by his friends, showing he has authority to forgive sins. He calls Levi, a tax collector, to follow him and eats with other tax collectors and sinners, explaining he came for those who need him, not the self-righteous. He also addresses questions about fasting and defends his disciples for picking grain on the Sabbath, declaring that the Sabbath was made for people, not people for the Sabbath.
chapters.3: Jesus heals a man's withered hand on the Sabbath, angering religious leaders who begin plotting against him. As crowds grow, he appoints twelve apostles to be with him and to preach and heal. When accused of casting out demons by the power of Satan, he answers that a divided kingdom cannot stand, warns about blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, and redefines family as whoever does God's will.
chapters.4: Jesus teaches in parables, starting with the parable of the sower and explaining how different hearts receive God's word differently. He adds short parables about a lamp on a stand, seed growing secretly, and a mustard seed becoming a large plant, all describing the hidden but certain growth of God's kingdom. The chapter ends with Jesus calming a violent storm on the sea with a word, astonishing his disciples.
chapters.5: Jesus delivers a man possessed by many demons ('Legion') near the tombs, sending the spirits into a herd of pigs that rushes into the sea. On returning across the lake, a woman who has suffered bleeding for twelve years is healed simply by touching his garment in faith. He then raises Jairus's twelve-year-old daughter from death, telling onlookers she was only sleeping.
chapters.6: Jesus is rejected by the people of his own hometown, Nazareth, who can't see past the carpenter they grew up with. He sends his twelve disciples out in pairs to preach and heal, and the chapter recounts how Herod had earlier had John the Baptist beheaded after a rash promise to his stepdaughter. Jesus then feeds five thousand people with five loaves and two fish, walks on water to his disciples during a storm, and heals many more people when he reaches shore.
chapters.7: Jesus challenges the Pharisees' obsession with ritual hand-washing, teaching that true defilement comes from what's in a person's heart, not external rules. A Gentile woman from Syrophoenicia persistently pleads for her daughter's healing, and Jesus commends her faith and frees the girl from a demon. He also heals a deaf man who could barely speak, restoring his hearing and speech.
chapters.8: Jesus feeds four thousand people with seven loaves and a few fish, then warns his disciples against the corrupting influence ('leaven') of the Pharisees and of Herod. After healing a blind man at Bethsaida, he asks the disciples who they think he is; Peter declares him the Christ, and Jesus begins openly predicting his coming death and resurrection, rebuking Peter for resisting the idea. He then teaches that following him means denying oneself and being willing to lose one's life for his sake.
chapters.9: Jesus is transfigured on a mountain before Peter, James, and John, appearing in radiant glory alongside Moses and Elijah while God's voice confirms him as his Son. Coming down, he heals a boy with a violent, mute spirit that the disciples had failed to cast out, telling them this kind requires prayer. He again predicts his death and resurrection, and teaches the disciples (who had been arguing about greatness) that true greatness means serving others and welcoming the vulnerable like children.
chapters.10: Jesus teaches on the permanence of marriage, welcomes children as models of the kingdom, and tells a rich man to sell his possessions and follow him, teaching that wealth makes it hard to enter God's kingdom. He predicts his death a third time, and when James and John ask for places of honor, he teaches that true greatness in his kingdom means serving others, just as he came to serve. The chapter ends with Jesus healing the blind beggar Bartimaeus near Jericho.
chapters.11: Jesus rides into Jerusalem on a colt to shouts of 'Hosanna' from the crowd, fulfilling a prophetic, kingly entrance. The next day he curses a fruitless fig tree and drives merchants and money-changers out of the temple, condemning what should be a house of prayer. When religious leaders question his authority, he responds with a question of his own about John the Baptist that leaves them unable to answer.
chapters.12: Jesus tells the parable of the wicked tenants who kill the vineyard owner's son, a pointed warning to the religious leaders plotting against him. He skillfully answers traps about paying taxes to Caesar and about the resurrection, and names loving God and loving one's neighbor as the greatest commandments. He also warns against the showy hypocrisy of the religious elite and praises a poor widow whose small offering, given out of true devotion, outweighs the large gifts of the wealthy.
chapters.13: Jesus predicts the destruction of the Jerusalem temple and, in response to the disciples' questions, describes signs that will precede great upheaval: wars, earthquakes, persecution, and false prophets. He speaks of a coming 'abomination of desolation' and intense tribulation, followed by the Son of Man's return in glory to gather his people. He closes by urging constant watchfulness, since no one knows the exact time these events will happen.
chapters.14: A woman anoints Jesus with expensive perfume at Bethany as an act of devotion before his burial, while Judas secretly arranges to betray him to the religious leaders. At the Passover meal, Jesus institutes what becomes the Lord's Supper, identifying the bread and cup with his body and blood, and predicts Peter's denial. In Gethsemane he prays in anguish before his arrest, and is taken before the high priest, who condemns him for claiming to be the Christ, while Peter denies knowing him three times as predicted.
chapters.15: Jesus is brought before Pilate, who offers to release him but instead releases the criminal Barabbas after the crowd, stirred up by the chief priests, demands Jesus be crucified. Roman soldiers mock and beat him before crucifying him between two criminals, and he dies after several hours, causing the temple curtain to tear and a Roman centurion to declare him the Son of God. Joseph of Arimathea obtains Pilate's permission to bury Jesus' body in a rock-cut tomb.
chapters.16: Women arriving at the tomb on the third day find the stone rolled away and are told by an angelic figure that Jesus has risen. Jesus then appears alive to Mary Magdalene and to others, though the disciples at first struggle to believe the reports. He commissions the eleven to go and preach the gospel to the whole world before being taken up into heaven.
